newsitem.title: GERMANY: Aluminium seen vulnerable to future price spikes.
newsitem.headline: Aluminium seen vulnerable to future price spikes.

text.p: Aluminium supply deficits may develop over the next few years, causing sharp price spikes, analyst Anthony Bird told a Metal Bulletin conference on Monday.
The impact of recent low prices on plans for new production projects meant markets were ill prepared for any surges in demand and a likely decline in former Soviet Union export availability, he said.
Western world demand growth in 1990-2006 might exceed the 1990-1995 annual average of 3.3 percent, to reach 3.6 percent
By contrast, western capacity had risen by 1.9 percent in 1990-1995 and was set to grow by just 1.5 percent in 1995-2001.
That forecast assumed all existing smelters stayed in business, which was by no means guaranteed.
Since 1982, some 35 western world smelters representing 20 percent of total capacity had been shut down.
Although the rate of closures would now slow, new net capacity additions would take a "very sedate pace indeed -- about 0.5 percent a year," he said.
If capacity expansions elsewhere were added, total supply growth would in theory be higher, but Russian plants were old and inefficient and many small Chinese smelters needed replacing.
The industry was lean following voluntary producer shutdowns, and capacity utilisation during the current market trough was 92 percent, compared with 73 percent in 1982.
"A boom patch means trouble," Bird said, adding, "It would be hard to operate a smelter for long at more than 95 percent."
Commonwalth of Independent States (CIS) demand had plunged 80 percent in the past five years as local industries collapsed but this process would come to an end.
